title: Not Nvidia. Not Micron. If I Could Buy and Hold Only 1 Artificial Intelligence (AI) Semiconductor Stock Through 2030, This Would Be It. - The Globe and Mail
content: Nvidia and Micron face rising competition in their respective pockets of the chip ecosystem. Taiwan Semiconductor benefits from demand across various chip architectures. TSMC's near-monopolistic position and attractive valuation make it a compelling long-term investment. For much of the last four years, semiconductor stocks have been some of the biggest beneficiaries of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. While Nvidia(NASDAQ:NVDA) has become the king of AI accelerators, Micron Technology(NASDAQ:MU) is capitalizing on unprecedented demand for memory chips. Although both companies have attractive long-term growth prospects, competition could complicate their investment narratives over the next several years. Moreover, as the AI infrastructure landscape evolves, identifying which chip architectures will dominate the market is becoming more challenging. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Fortunately, there's one semiconductor company that stands to benefit from virtually every major development across the AI chip landscape: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM). Between its graphics processing units (GPUs), networking equipment, and CUDA software ecosystem, Nvidia has an exceptionally durable competitive moat. Nevertheless, Advanced Micro Devices is investing aggressively in its Instinct accelerator portfolio, while some of Nvidia's largest customers are developing custom silicon. Broadcom has emerged as an important partner in the market for application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), most notably through its relationship with Alphabet and its tensor processing units (TPUs). Meanwhile, Microsoft and Amazon are also developing their own chip portfolios, including Maia, Trainium, and Inferentia. Another potential source of competition is Space Exploration Technologies' collaboration with Intel on Terafab. Terafab is Elon Musk's semiconductor manufacturing initiative that could eventually reduce SpaceX's dependence on third-party chip suppliers. Although commercial-scale production remains uncertain, the project underscores a growing appetite for vertically integrated semiconductor solutions. Micron faces a different set of challenges. While the proliferation of generative AI has ushered in a memory supercycle, memory-intensive applications such as humanoid robotics and autonomous vehicles should introduce additional tailwinds over the next several years. However, Micron competes against Samsung and SK Hynix in the high bandwidth memory (HBM) market. Furthermore, memory pricing has historically been cyclical, leaving producers vulnerable to fluctuations in supply, demand, and profitability. While Nvidia and Micron could both continue thriving, there is an alternative way to invest in the semiconductor industry without betting on a particular chip designer or memory manufacturer. Unlike Nvidia and AMD, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSMC) primarily manufactures semiconductors designed by other companies. Its customer base includes businesses spanning GPUs, custom AI accelerators, smartphone processors, and automotive chips. Against this backdrop, if Nvidia continues to dominate the AI accelerator market, TSMC benefits. Should AMD start to capture additional market share or custom ASICs become increasingly popular, TSMC still stands to benefit because it manufactures chips across these competing architectures as well. Interestingly, Taiwan Semi also has exposure to the memory supercycle. While the company isn't a producer of conventional dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), its collaboration with SK Hynix involves manufacturing logic base dies for next-generation HBM4 solutions. Moreover, TSMC's advanced packaging technologies -- particularly its chip-on-wafer-on-substrate (CoWoS) platform -- play a critical role in integrating AI processors with HBM. As a result, growing demand for more sophisticated memory configurations creates additional markets for TSMC beyond traditional wafer fabrication. The most compelling aspect of TSMC's competitive positioning is the sheer magnitude of its market share. Industry estimates suggest that Taiwan Semi controls roughly 73% of the global pure-play foundry market. By contrast, the next closest competitor sits at just 6%. Although TSMC isn't technically a monopoly, its dominance gives it the characteristics of one. The company's manufacturing expertise, technological edge, production scale, and customer relationships are simply too difficult for the competition to replicate at scale. During the third quarter, Taiwan Semi generated $46.7 billion in revenue, representing 41% year-over-year growth. Meanwhile, the company's gross margin reached nearly 65%, and its operating margin expanded to about 59%. Management expects revenue to reach $53.3 billion in the fourth quarter, implying 58% year-over-year growth. These results illustrate how TSMC's manufacturing scale is translating insatiable semiconductor demand into robust profitability. Despite these impressive financial trends, Taiwan Semi stock trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E)ratio of 15.7. That valuation profile looks attractive for a business generating this level of growth and profitability while commanding such a dominant market position. Rather than attempting to identify which chip designer or memory producer will emerge victorious over the next several years, investing in the company that manufactures many of the industry's most in-demand products looks like a compelling strategy. TSMC's architecture-agnostic business model, durable competitive advantages, and reasonable valuation make it a compelling semiconductor stock to buy now and hold through the end of the decade. title: Billionaire Stanley Druckenmiller Sold 94% of His TSMC Stake and All of His Alphabet Shares in Q3. Here’s the Brilliant Stock He Added. - The Motley Fool
content: The market has changed since these moves were made. With the latest rounds of 13Fs out, investors get to see what billionaire hedge fund managers were up to in the third quarter. One investor I follow is Stanley Druckenmiller, who runs the Duquesne Family Office. Druckenmiller has a strong history of picking great stocks, and he made some interesting moves in Q3. But should you follow his lead? Let's take a look at what he did. Druckenmiller hasn't allocated a large portion of his portfolio to AI-related stocks, and in Q3, he sold two prominent ones. He fully exited his 336,300-share position in Alphabet (GOOG -2.02%) (GOOGL -2.13%), which is actually something he has done before. He held Alphabet shares in Q4 2025, then sold that position entirely in Q1 before buying the stock again in Q2. With Alphabet being one of the poster children for the AI build-out, this sale is notable. Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM -1.96%) is another company often cited as one of the best AI investments, as it manufactures the lion’s share of the high-end chips that end up in nearly every AI computing unit. It has had tremendous returns over the past few years, and Druckenmiller has maintained a large position since Q4 of last year. However, he sold off around 94% of his TSMC holdings — his No. 2 position as of the end of Q2 — and he may close it fully in Q4 (if he hasn't bought any recently). Those were two notable sales, but what did he buy instead? Druckenmiller added a fair bit of Amazon (AMZN -3.12%) stock to his portfolio during Q3, bringing it from his ninth-largest position to his third-largest position. Amazon is still somewhat of an AI investment, as it gets a hefty chunk of its operating profit from its cloud computing division, Amazon Web Services (AWS). AWS has seen its growth rate boosted by rising cloud workloads, driven by increased AI usage. These were some interesting moves by Druckenmiller, but is that still the right plan? I'd say no. These holdings were as of Sept. 30, and a lot has shifted in the market since then. Since Q3 ended, Amazon has essentially been flat. Meanwhile, Alphabet has sold off by more than 20%, while Taiwan Semiconductor is down by 30%. Those were major declines, and Druckenmiller got out ahead of them, which suggests that he saw which way the wind would be blowing. However, selling those stocks now could be a mistake because the prices are so much lower. In fact, Druckenmiller could be buying those two stocks back right now, but we won't know until Q4 data is released in mid-February. With that in mind, I think investors should consider doing at this point the exact opposite of what the Duquesne Family Office did in Q3, as the landscape has shifted over the past month and a half. The gain followed a 9.48% drop to $318.71 on Friday, November 20. Those shares are an American depository receipt (ADR), a U.S.-traded certificate backed by stock listed in Taipei. Monday was the ADR’s biggest one-day percentage gain since October 28, 2008, when it rose 21.07%. 2026's Biggest AI Trends: The Memory Explosion | MU Stock, SNDK Stock, SK Hynix, CAMT Stock The jump came the day Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) named Jensen Huang as CEO, and the stock closed up 31.48%. The question for shareholders is whether one big session can repair a stock that still closed about 25% below its record close of $485.80 on October 5, 2026, even as revenue kept rising. The ADR hit $386.90 early, about 21.4% above Friday’s close. By the end of the day, it had slid to just above the session low of $361.66. The Taiwan-listed shares closed up 1.50% at NT$2,030. Their session ended at 1:30 p.m. Taipei time, or 12:30 a.m. ET Monday, hours before Nvidia’s announcement. The same company can post two very different daily moves because the two markets trade at different hours. Taipei’s November 24 session was the first chance for those shares to respond. After hours at 7:39 p.m. ET Monday, the ADR traded at $368.69, up another 1.40%. After-hours prices can change before the next open. Monday ranks 11th among the ADR’s daily gains since October 1997. All ten bigger gains came between 1997 and 2002 or on October 28, 2008. Those periods covered the Asian financial crisis, the dot-com collapse and the worst of the global financial crisis. The largest up days tend to come in violent markets, usually right after sharp drops, when short sellers rush to buy back shares.
